title: Hypothesis: beta-adrenergic receptor blockers and weight gain: a systematic analysis
authors: Sharma AM, Pischon T, Hardt S, Kunz I, Luft FC
population: Eight evaluable prospective randomised controlled trials of beta-blockers in hypertension lasting at least 6 months that reported body weight
funder: not stated; the archived full text carries no funding statement.
result: Body weight at the end of the trials was higher with a beta-blocker than in the control group, median difference 1.2 kg (range -0.4 to 3.5 kg). Regression suggested weight gain in the first few months and none thereafter against controls, without relation to demographic characteristics. The review cites studies in which beta-blockers lowered total energy expenditure by 4% to 9%, and the authors' own finding of a 12% lower basal metabolic rate in obese hypertensive patients on beta-blockers, and notes that beta-blockade inhibits adrenergically stimulated lipolysis. The authors state that effects on body weight are generally ignored in randomised studies of antihypertensive medication and that there is little information on the effects of antihypertensive beta-blockers on beta3-adrenoceptor-mediated energy expenditure.
